The Edusim Stages Project Database

61 projects to play, read and remix, for grades 3 to 12: science, maths, history, art and language, each made with blocks. Open one, press the green flag, then look inside: every script is there to read and change. Free, in the browser, with no account.

🌍 Earth & SpaceSimulation · Grades 3–5

The Water Cycle

Heat the sea, build a cloud, make it rain. Click the Sun to turn up the heat.

You'll learn: The four stages of the water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, and why the Sun drives all of them.

▶ Open The Water Cycle ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceSimulation · Grades 4–8

A Volcano with Lava

Press space to heat the magma. When the pressure gets too high, it erupts, and the lava cools into rock.

You'll learn: How gas pressure in magma drives an eruption, the difference between magma and lava, and how cooling lava becomes igneous rock.

▶ Open A Volcano with Lava ↗

🎨 Art & MusicArt · Grades 3–8

Da Vinci's Paint Shop

Paint on Leonardo's easel. Dip in two primary colours to mix a new one, and ask Leonardo about his work.

You'll learn: Primary and secondary colours (red + yellow = orange, yellow + blue = green, blue + red = purple), and who Leonardo da Vinci was: painter, inventor and notebook-keeper.

▶ Open Da Vinci's Paint Shop ↗

🦋 Life ScienceGame · Grades 3–5

A Butterfly Garden

Watch an egg become a butterfly, then fly it with the mouse from flower to flower to spread pollen.

You'll learn: The four stages of complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult), and how butterflies pollinate flowers while drinking nectar.

▶ Open A Butterfly Garden ↗

🦋 Life ScienceQuiz · Grades 6–8

Inside an Animal Cell

Click each part of the cell to find out its job, then press Q to test yourself.

You'll learn: The main organelles of an animal cell and what each one does: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and the cell membrane.

▶ Open Inside an Animal Cell ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceSimulation · Grades 3–5

Phases of the Moon

Move the Moon around Earth and watch it change from new to full and back again.

You'll learn: Why the Moon has phases: the Sun always lights half of it, and as it orbits Earth we see more or less of that lit half. The eight phase names, and that a full cycle takes about 29.5 days.

▶ Open Phases of the Moon ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceGame · Grades 3–5

Planet Parade

The planets are all mixed up! Click them in order from the Sun outwards to line them up.

You'll learn: The order of the eight planets from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), a memory trick for it, and one big fact about each planet.

▶ Open Planet Parade ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceGame · Grades 3–6

The Rock Cycle

Melt it, cool it, wear it away, squeeze it, heat it. Can you turn one rock into all three kinds?

You'll learn: The three kinds of rock (igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic), the processes that turn one into another (melting, cooling, weathering and erosion, compaction and cementing, heat and pressure), and that the cycle never stops.

▶ Open The Rock Cycle ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceSimulation · Grades 5–8

Why We Have Seasons

Take Earth round the Sun and watch the tilted axis. Then see how high the noon Sun climbs in each season.

You'll learn: Seasons come from Earth's tilt of about 23.5°, not from its distance to the Sun: the hemisphere leaning toward the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days. Solstices, equinoxes, and why Australia's seasons are the other way round.

▶ Open Why We Have Seasons ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceAnimation · Grades 6–8

Plates on the Move

Earth's crust is cracked into plates. Pull them apart, push them together, or slide them past each other and see what happens.

You'll learn: Plate tectonics: the three kinds of plate boundary (divergent, convergent, transform), what each one builds (new ocean floor, volcanoes and mountains, earthquake faults), and that the mantle moves the plates a few centimetres a year.

▶ Open Plates on the Move ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceQuiz · Grades 6–8

Layers of the Atmosphere

Fly a rocket up through the five layers of the air, from the clouds to the edge of space. Then take the quiz.

You'll learn: The five layers of the atmosphere in order (troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere), roughly how high each reaches, what happens in each (weather, the ozone layer, meteors, auroras), and how the temperature goes down, up, down and up again.

▶ Open Layers of the Atmosphere ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceSimulation · Grades 9–12

Kepler's Orbits

Launch a planet around the Sun with real gravity. Change its speed and watch the ellipse, the speed and the orbit time.

You'll learn: Newton's inverse-square gravity, stepped one frame at a time, produces Kepler's three laws: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus, a planet moves fastest when closest to the Sun (equal areas in equal times), and bigger orbits take longer (T² is proportional to a³).

▶ Open Kepler's Orbits ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceStory · Grades 8–12

The Life of a Star

Follow a star from a cloud of dust to its end. A star like our Sun fades gently; a giant star explodes.

You'll learn: The life cycle of stars: nebula, protostar and main sequence for every star; then red giant, planetary nebula and white dwarf for a Sun-like star, or red supergiant, supernova and a neutron star or black hole for a star more than about 8 times the Sun's mass. Why mass decides how a star lives and dies.

▶ Open The Life of a Star ↗

🌍 Earth & SpaceSimulation · Grades 9–12

The Greenhouse Effect

Sunlight warms the ground; the ground glows infrared; greenhouse gases send some of it back. Add or remove gas and watch the warmth.

You'll learn: How the greenhouse effect works: visible sunlight passes through the air, the warm ground gives off infrared, and gases like carbon dioxide absorb it and send some back down, so the surface settles at a warmer balance. Why some greenhouse effect is essential, and how adding carbon dioxide has warmed Earth.

▶ Open The Greenhouse Effect ↗

🦋 Life ScienceQuiz · Grades 3–5

What Does Each Plant Part Do?

Click the roots, stem, leaves, flower and seeds to learn each one's job, then help the bee with a quiz.

You'll learn: The five main parts of a flowering plant and the job of each: roots take in water, the stem carries it, leaves make food by photosynthesis, flowers make seeds, and seeds grow into new plants.

▶ Open What Does Each Plant Part Do? ↗

🦋 Life ScienceStory · Grades 3–5

From Frogspawn to Frog

Watch an egg in a pond turn into a tadpole, a froglet and a frog, then help the frog catch flies.

You'll learn: The life cycle of a frog (frogspawn, tadpole, tadpole with legs, froglet, adult) and what "amphibian" means: an animal that starts life in water and lives on land as an adult.

▶ Open From Frogspawn to Frog ↗

🦋 Life ScienceGame · Grades 3–5

Sort the Animals

Is a whale a fish? Is a bat a bird? Click the right group for each animal and learn the clues.

You'll learn: The five groups of vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish), the features that put an animal in each group, and that every one of them has a backbone.

▶ Open Sort the Animals ↗

🦋 Life ScienceSimulation · Grades 6–8

Energy in a Food Chain

Send the Sun's energy up a food chain and watch the energy pyramid build, step by step. Then answer three questions.

You'll learn: How energy flows from the Sun through producers and consumers, why only about 10% passes to each next level (the rest is used or lost as heat), and what decomposers do.

▶ Open Energy in a Food Chain ↗

🦋 Life ScienceAnimation · Grades 6–8

The Journey of Your Lunch

Take a bite of a sandwich and follow it through the mouth, stomach and intestines, then answer three questions.

You'll learn: The organs of the digestive system in order (mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum), what happens in each, and how the liver and pancreas help.

▶ Open The Journey of Your Lunch ↗

🦋 Life ScienceGame · Grades 6–8

Germ Defenders

Germs got in through a cut! Steer a white blood cell to swallow them before they multiply, then unlock antibodies.

You'll learn: The body's defences against germs: skin as a barrier, white blood cells that swallow germs (phagocytes), antibodies that tag germs, and memory cells, which are how vaccines work.

▶ Open Germ Defenders ↗

🦋 Life ScienceSimulation · Grades 9–12

Rabbits and Foxes

A predator-prey model drawn live as a graph. Add rabbits or foxes and watch both populations rise and fall in waves.

You'll learn: How predator and prey populations depend on each other, why their numbers cycle with the predator peak lagging the prey peak, and how a simple mathematical model (Lotka-Volterra) can show it.

▶ Open Rabbits and Foxes ↗

🦋 Life ScienceQuiz · Grades 9–12

From DNA to Protein

Watch a gene copied into mRNA, then a ribosome read it three letters at a time to build a protein. Press M for a mutation.

You'll learn: How a gene becomes a protein: transcription (DNA to mRNA, with A-U, T-A, C-G, G-C pairing), translation at a ribosome (codons of three bases, each coding for an amino acid, with start and stop codons), and how one changed base can change a protein.

▶ Open From DNA to Protein ↗

🦋 Life ScienceSimulation · Grades 8–12

Peppered Moths: Natural Selection

Be a hungry bird and eat the moths you can see. Then soot blackens the trees, and watch the moths change over the generations.

You'll learn: How natural selection works: variation in a population, inheritance from parents, and predators removing the less well hidden, using the real story of peppered moths in industrial England.

▶ Open Peppered Moths: Natural Selection ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistryGame · Grades 3–5

Sink or Float?

Predict whether each thing will sink or float, then drop it in the tank and see if you were right.

You'll learn: Whether something floats depends on its density compared with water, not just on its size or weight: air inside makes things less dense, metal and rock are denser.

▶ Open Sink or Float? ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistryGame · Grades 3–5

Magnet Pick-Up

Drive a magnet with the arrow keys and find out what it picks up. Then see two magnets attract and repel.

You'll learn: Magnets pull on things made of iron and steel but not on wood, plastic or cloth; the pull gets stronger as they get closer; and opposite poles attract while like poles repel.

▶ Open Magnet Pick-Up ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistrySimulation · Grades 3–6

Light Up the Bulb

Close the switch and test things in the gap. Which ones let electricity through to light the bulb?

You'll learn: Electricity only flows around a complete loop called a circuit; a switch opens and closes the loop; metals are conductors and rubber, plastic and wool are insulators.

▶ Open Light Up the Bulb ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistryStory · Grades 5–8

Archimedes' Lever

Archimedes shows Maya how a plank and a pivot can lift a rock five times heavier than she is. Slide the fulcrum to do it.

You'll learn: A lever turns about a fulcrum, and its turning effect is weight times distance from the fulcrum. Move the fulcrum close to a heavy load and a small effort far away can lift it.

▶ Open Archimedes' Lever ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistrySimulation · Grades 6–8

Heat It Up: Ice, Water, Steam

Heat a jar of ice and watch its particles. Why does the thermometer stop at 0 °C and at 100 °C?

You'll learn: Solids, liquids and gases are the same particles moving in different ways; heating makes particles move faster; and while ice melts or water boils, the heat breaks particles apart instead of raising the temperature.

▶ Open Heat It Up: Ice, Water, Steam ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistryArt · Grades 6–8

Make a Wave: See Your Sound

Play notes and watch their sound waves. Higher notes squeeze the waves closer together; louder notes make them taller.

You'll learn: A sound has a frequency (how many waves pass each second, heard as pitch) and an amplitude (heard as loudness); because sound travels at about 343 m/s, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

▶ Open Make a Wave: See Your Sound ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistryGame · Grades 9–12

Cannonball Arc

Set the angle and speed, fire, and land the cannonball on the target. Every shot leaves its arc behind to compare.

You'll learn: A projectile moves at a steady speed sideways while gravity changes its upward speed by 9.8 m/s every second, which makes a parabola; on flat ground with no air resistance the range is v² sin(2θ) / g, longest at 45°.

▶ Open Cannonball Arc ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistrySimulation · Grades 9–12

The Pendulum Lab

Change the string, the weight of the bob and even the planet. What changes how long one swing takes?

You'll learn: A pendulum's period depends on its length and on gravity, T = 2π√(L/g), but not on its mass: four times the length doubles the period, and weaker gravity on the Moon or Mars slows it down.

▶ Open The Pendulum Lab ↗

⚛️ Physics & ChemistryQuiz · Grades 8–11

Build an Atom

Add protons, neutrons and electrons to build real atoms, isotopes and ions, then check your work.

You'll learn: The number of protons decides the element; protons + neutrons give the mass number; isotopes have different numbers of neutrons; and an ion has a charge because its electrons and protons do not balance.

▶ Open Build an Atom ↗

📐 MathGame · Grades 3–4

Pizza Fractions

Cut a pizza into equal slices, click slices to eat them, and see the fraction you ate. Press Q for a pizza quiz.

You'll learn: A fraction is part of a whole: the bottom number (denominator) is how many equal parts, the top number (numerator) is how many you have. Different fractions like 4/8 and 1/2 can be the same amount.

▶ Open Pizza Fractions ↗

📐 MathSimulation · Grades 3–4

The Array Garden

Plant flowers in rows and columns. Change the rows and columns with the arrow keys and count by rows to multiply.

You'll learn: Multiplication as an array: rows × columns = total. Skip counting by rows gives the same answer, turning the array round (3 × 5 and 5 × 3) does not change the product, and an array can show division too.

▶ Open The Array Garden ↗

📐 MathGame · Grades 3–5

Frog Hops the Number Line

Help a hungry frog catch flies by typing how far to hop. Plus hops right, minus hops left.

You'll learn: Adding moves right on a number line and subtracting moves left. The distance between two numbers is the bigger one minus the smaller one, so to get from 4 to 11 you add 11 − 4 = 7.

▶ Open Frog Hops the Number Line ↗

📐 MathQuiz · Grades 5–7

Pirate Coordinates

Read the coordinates of four hidden gems on a treasure map. Type x, then y, and the X walks there to dig.

You'll learn: Every point on the coordinate plane is an ordered pair (x, y): x first, left or right of the origin, then y, up or down. Negative numbers go left and down, and the signs tell you which of the four quadrants a point is in.

▶ Open Pirate Coordinates ↗

📐 MathArt · Grades 5–8

The Polygon Turtle

A turtle draws any regular polygon, or a star, by walking and turning. Find out why the turns always add up to 360°.

You'll learn: To draw a regular polygon you turn 360 ÷ (number of sides) at every corner (the exterior angle). The interior angle is 180° minus that, and the interior angles add up to (sides − 2) × 180°. A star turns twice as far, 720° in all.

▶ Open The Polygon Turtle ↗

📐 MathStory · Grades 6–7

Smoothie Ratios

Leo's smoothie stand uses 2 bananas for every 3 strawberries. Scale the recipe up to serve hungry animal customers.

You'll learn: A ratio compares two amounts, like 2 bananas : 3 strawberries. Multiplying both parts by the same number makes an equivalent ratio (4 : 6, 6 : 9), which is how you scale a recipe up and still get the same taste.

▶ Open Smoothie Ratios ↗

📐 MathSimulation · Grades 7–10

Roll Two Dice

Roll two dice hundreds of times and watch a bar chart grow. Why does 7 come up so much more than 2 or 12?

You'll learn: Experimental and theoretical probability. Two dice can land 36 equally likely ways; 6 of them total 7 but only 1 totals 2, so P(7) = 6/36 ≈ 16.7%. The more you roll, the closer the results come to the theory (the law of large numbers).

▶ Open Roll Two Dice ↗

📐 MathGame · Grades 8–10

Line Up: y = mx + b

Steer a line through two stars by changing its slope m and its y-intercept b. Four missions, from steep to flat.

You'll learn: In y = mx + b, b is where the line crosses the y-axis and m is the slope: how far the line rises for every 1 step to the right (rise ÷ run). A negative slope falls, and a slope of 0 is a flat line.

▶ Open Line Up: y = mx + b ↗

📐 MathAnimation · Grades 10–12

The Sine Wave Machine

A dot goes round a circle while a pen plots its height. Out comes a sine wave. Press C for cosine, UP/DOWN to change the size.

You'll learn: On the unit circle the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), so sin θ is its height and cos θ is how far across it is. Plotting the height against θ draws a sine wave that repeats every 360°; a bigger circle gives a bigger amplitude.

▶ Open The Sine Wave Machine ↗

🏛️ History & GeographyArt · Grades 3–5

Write Like an Egyptian Scribe

Type your name and a scribe writes it in hieroglyphs, inside a royal cartouche.

You'll learn: Ancient Egyptians wrote with picture signs called hieroglyphs, many of which stood for sounds, and royal names were written inside an oval rope called a cartouche.

▶ Open Write Like an Egyptian Scribe ↗

🏛️ History & GeographyGame · Grades 6–8

The Silk Roads

Lead a camel caravan from Chang'an in China to Constantinople, trading goods and ideas at every oasis city.

You'll learn: The Silk Roads were a web of trade routes linking China with western Asia and Europe for about 1,500 years, carrying goods like silk and paper, and ideas and religions too.

▶ Open The Silk Roads ↗

🏛️ History & GeographySimulation · Grades 9–12

Longitude by the Clock

Find two lost ships the way 18th-century navigators did: latitude from the North Star, longitude from a clock.

You'll learn: Latitude and longitude as angles; how the height of Polaris gives latitude; and how Earth turning 15° an hour lets a clock set to Greenwich time give longitude, the problem John Harrison's sea clocks solved.

▶ Open Longitude by the Clock ↗

🎨 Art & MusicGame · Grades 3–5

Melody Maker

Play a rainbow keyboard with the mouse or the A to K keys, hear famous tunes, then write your own song in letters.

You'll learn: Notes have letter names, C D E F G A B C is a scale that climbs in pitch, an octave is eight notes up, and rhythm is how long each note lasts.

▶ Open Melody Maker ↗

🎨 Art & MusicSimulation · Grades 6–8

The Colour Wheel

Spin the pointer round the painter's colour wheel and see every colour beside its complement, then take the quiz.

You'll learn: Primary, secondary and tertiary colours on the painter's wheel, and complementary colours: opposites that make each other look brighter side by side and turn brown or grey when mixed.

▶ Open The Colour Wheel ↗

🎨 Art & MusicArt · Grades 9–12

Seurat's Dots

Watch a park scene appear from thousands of dots of pure colour, then dab your own and see the colours mix in your eye.

You'll learn: Pointillism, the Neo-Impressionist method Georges Seurat developed in the 1880s: small dots of unmixed colour placed side by side, so the colours blend in the viewer's eye rather than on the palette.

▶ Open Seurat's Dots ↗

📖 Language ArtsAnimation · Grades 3–5

The Sentence Machine

Click the word cards to build a silly sentence, then watch it acted out: tiny dragons, giant penguins, robots that sing.

You'll learn: The parts of speech in a sentence: nouns name things, verbs are actions, adjectives describe nouns and adverbs describe how the action happens.

▶ Open The Sentence Machine ↗

📖 Language ArtsStory · Grades 6–8

Haiku Garden

Click each line of a poem to change it, then clap out the syllables. Get 5-7-5 and the cherry blossoms fall.

You'll learn: What a syllable is and how to count one by clapping, and the form of a haiku: three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables in English, often with a word for a season.

▶ Open Haiku Garden ↗

📖 Language ArtsQuiz · Grades 9–12

Ethos, Pathos, Logos

Six persuasive messages, three ways to persuade. Sort each one: does it lean on trust, feelings, or reasons?

You'll learn: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion: ethos (the speaker's credibility), pathos (the audience's emotions) and logos (logic and evidence), and how to spot which one an argument is using.

▶ Open Ethos, Pathos, Logos ↗

For teachers

Every project here is made by Edusim, and the Project Database inside the app holds the same list. Each one opens in Edusim Stages with its scripts showing, so a class can play it, explain how it works, then change it: make the Sun hotter, add a planet, write a new quiz question. Projects are kept in the student's own browser; nothing is uploaded. See the Stages guide for step-by-step tutorials.
